author: Emma Honeybun
title: Public Safety minister appoints full time correctional investigator
content:
The federal government has appointed the new head at the Office of the Correctional Investigator, it announced Tuesday.




This will be the permanent successor to Ivan Zinger, who took his early retirement in February 2026, two years before his position expired.




The position was left vacant for four months until Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree appointed an interim commissioner.




David Paradiso, the deputy Ombudsman in B.C. will take the seat on Oct. 13.




Canada’s correctional investigator works as an independent watchdog for the federal corrections system, investigating submitted complaints and concerns that have to do with living conditions, overpopulation, and several other issues faced by incarcerated people in federal prisons.




Paradiso has been the deputy 

British Columbia Ombudsperson

 since 2014, and, according to Canada, has “35 years of experience in public sector oversight, legal analysis, and independent investigations.”




According to the 

Forum of Canadian Ombudsman

, he helped establish the national Ombudsman for Canada Post and then spent time at the RCMP Public Complaint Commission.




He served as director of investigations with the Office of the Correctional Investigator [OCI] for six years and handled complaints and allegations from or concerning those in incarceration.

author: Sara Connors
title: Yukon Women’s Coalition raises alarm over RCMP incident at Whitehorse shelter
content:
A women’s coalition in the Yukon says it has serious concerns about an alleged excessive use of force incident last month involving an RCMP officer and a woman accessing services at a Whitehorse shelter.




According to 

new details released last week

 by the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team, or ASIRT, which is investigating the 

Aug. 11 incident

, an RCMP officer dragged a woman out of the Whitehorse emergency shelter and left her outside on the sidewalk.




The details also state there were no beds available at the shelter for the woman to stay overnight.




The 

Yukon Women’s Coalition

, a group of 10 women-led and feminist not-for-profit organizations, said in a 

Sept. 28 release

 that it’s “deeply concerned” about the incident and the new details that have been released.




“The details released thus far are deeply troubling and raise serious concerns about the dignity, safety and human rights of the woman involved, as well as the treatment of people accessing emergency shelter and other essential services,” it states.




“We are particularly concerned by the reported treatment of the woman by the RCMP member under investigation, and all circumstances surrounding the incident, including the apparent lack of available safe shelter space. There are many unanswered questions; however, it seems clear that this person has been systematically failed,” it adds.

author: Leanne Sanders
title: Expert on white nationalism in Canada disturbed, not surprised by demonstration at Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc
content:
A public demonstration by the white nationalist group Second Sons of Canada on land near the Kamloops residential school site over the weekend sent shockwaves across the country. For people who study the group and others like it, it was not surprising.




“White Nationalism 3.0 has emerged as a unifying organizational model within Canada’s white supremacist ecosystem,” wrote Steven Rai in

 Tribe and Train

,

 a March 2026 article which examined “Canada’s new model of white supremacist mobilization.”




Photos circulating Sunday showed men in black clothing, white face coverings and matching caps on the 

Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc

 reserve, some with flags. A later image appears to show the same group on the Pacific Way overpass in Kamloops holding a banner that read “Got Bones?”




“Despite frequent rebranding and occasional infighting, groups that have adopted this model (including 

Second Sons

 of Canada and the so-called Active Clubs) share a common strategy, unifying a previously fractured movement. This has allowed them to foster sustained growth since their emergence in Canada in 2021,” Rai, a senior research manager at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue Canada (ISD), wrote. ISD provides ” threat detection, analysis and real-world strategies to combat terrorism, extremism and authoritarianism – in all their ideological forms,” according to its website.

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: Kebaowek Nation pulls out of nuclear consultations, saying other parties failed
content:
Kebaowek First Nation announced Tuesday that it is suspending consultations on the proposed nuclear waste dump near its territory after it says the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC) and Canadian Nuclear Laboratories (CNL) “failed to meet critical commitments.”




According to a press release from Kebaowek First Nation, CNSC and CNL informed Kebaowek leadership that they would “no longer fund the Nation’s participation costs as previously understood,” and also that they would “end their participation in the co-development of a consent-based agreement to support the process.”




In 

a decision in February 2025

, Federal Court Justice Julie Blackhawk found that the CNSC failed to consider the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples in developing plans for nuclear waste dump in Kebaowek’s ancestral territory. Blackhawk ordered CNSC and CNL to consult with Kebaowek through an Indigenous-led Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) process. That FPIC process has also been suspended as a result of Kebaowek’s ending consultations.




In a statement emailed to APTN News, CNL representatives said they have engaged with Kebaowek and its representatives for 19 months in accordance with Federal Court instructions.

author: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs
title: Indian hospital survivors shape future of $385M foundation as northern claimants navigate compensation process
content:
For decades, Indigenous patients were sent to federally operated hospitals where they could be segregated from other patients and subjected to psychological, verbal, physical and sexual abuse; now, survivors are being asked what should happen next.




The Federal Court approved a settlement June 24, 2025, involving 33 Indian hospitals operated by the federal government at various times between 1936 and 1981.




The 

settlement

 provides individual compensation to eligible primary class members and establishes a $385.5 million foundation intended to support healing, research, education and commemoration.




The claims process and work to establish the foundation are happening at the same time, but they serve different purposes.




For northern claimants, accessing compensation can come with additional barriers.




Public awareness




Dr. Mike DeGagné, who is leading engagement sessions with the Indian Hospital Engagement Foundation for the future foundation, said Survivors have an opportunity to help shape what it should look like.




“If I go somewhere in Canada and I mention Indian residential schools, everybody sort of knows what I’m talking about, but if I say Indian hospitals, often they have no idea,” DeGagné said.




That lack of public awareness was a focus of a Yellowknife engagement session Sept. 22, one of a series being held across Canada.

author: The Canadian Press
title: Manitoba to purchase private campground near site of former residential school
content:
The Manitoba government is partnering with the province’s second-largest city to purchase a private campground where historical records show a cemetery for children who died at a residential school is located.




Premier Wab Kinew announced his government is working with the city of Brandon to acquire the Turtle Crossing Campground site, located south of the former Brandon Indian Residential School in western Manitoba.




A news release says the cemetery was used from 1985 to 1912 after the area was converted into a suburban park.




First Nations groups have long advocated for a search of the area to determine how many children were buried in the area and their identities.




Kinew says any future decisions regarding the site will be be done in consultation with residential school survivors, impacted First Nations and advocacy groups.




Chief Jennifer Bone of Sioux Valley Dakota Nation says any searches will be Indigenous-led and technical expertise and community knowledge will help guide the work.




“This is important work for our nation and for Indigenous Peoples across Canada,” she said in a joint statement with the province.




The First Nation previously worked with researchers to investigate unmarked graves at the former Brandon Indian Residential School.




It has said more than 50 are on the campground.

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: Indigenous services minister ‘disgusted and appalled’ after masked gathering on Tk’emlúps land
content:
Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty says she is “absolutely disgusted and appalled” after seeing a photograph of masked men who appeared on Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc land Sunday, three days before the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.




Gull-Masty, a Cree woman from Waswanipi and the first Indigenous person to hold the Indigenous Services portfolio, spoke at the National Indigenous Collaborative Housing Incorporated (NICHI) on Monday and was asked about the incident.




“I’m really disturbed by the level of comfort that I see in the behaviour that’s been carried out,” she said. “I haven’t had the opportunity to receive my briefing. I can’t comment on exactly what happened. I haven’t received the details of that activity yet.




“But I can confidently say that I’m absolutely disgusted and appalled.”




The white nationalist group, Second Sons Canada, gathered in Kamloops on Sunday. Photo: Facebook.







Kamloops Indian Residential School 




Kúkwpi7 (chief) Rosanne Casimir said in a Sunday statement that “individuals associated with Second Sons Canada, a group linked to white supremacist and white nationalist ideology, have been seen and documented within our community.”

author: Leanne Sanders
title: Elections Alberta reports more than 655,000 requests for special ballots for Oct. 19 referendum
content:
There appears to be high voter interest in the Alberta referendum on Oct. 19 which will decide whether the province should pursue the formal process to separate from Canada.




“We received approximately 658,000 requests for special ballots,” an Elections Alberta news release said. “This is more than 11 times as many requests as the 2023 Provincial General Election, where we received 59,589 special ballot requests.”




Elections Alberta attributed the increase to “the new availability of special ballot voting to all eligible electors without a reason, that voters must vote within their Electoral Division for Advance Vote or at their assigned location for Election Day, voter interest, and the number of questions electors must vote on.”




More than 82 per cent of the special ballots have been approved for fulfilment and mailing, it noted, with “0.7 per cent rejected either at application or on return, and nearly 100,000 have been received back and approved, and those electors marked as voted.”




It also expects the “total requests number will change as all final requests received before the deadline are entered into the system.”




Treaty 8 Sovereign Nations in Alberta is reminding members that if they requested a special ballot, they must vote that way and not in person.

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Sister of late Russell Woodhouse wants to set record straight on 1973 manslaughter charge: affidavit
content:
The younger sister of a First Nations man convicted of manslaughter in the 1970s has taken his case back to the Manitoba Court of Appeal 15 years after his death.




Russell Woodhouse, a member of Pinaymootang First Nation, was one of four to receive sentences following the 1973 Winnipeg murder of Ting Fong Chan.




While Woodhouse received 10 years in prison for manslaughter, his brother, Clarence Woodhouse; cousin, Brian Anderson; and fellow community member Allan Woodhouse (unrelated), were convicted of murder and sentenced to life in prison.




Innocence Canada, a legal non-profit organization that advocates for the exoneration of individuals who have been wrongly convicted, began to file applications to review the murder cases in 2019.




In 2023, Anderson and Allan Woodhouse were acquitted. Clarence Woodhouse was acquitted soon after, in 2024.




Now, Lisa Anderson, Russel and Clarence’s youngest sister, is returning to the Court of Appeal to have the outstanding case reassessed.




Lisa chose to take his place in court as his next of kin. He died of cancer in 2011, and the two “were always very close and remained close” until his death, she wrote in an affidavit filed in Winnipeg on Thursday.

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: CAP national chief says $3M cut of federal money came without notice
content:
The 

Congress of Aboriginal Peoples (CAP)

 says the federal government has unilaterally ended the Canada-CAP Political Accord and cut about $3 million a year in funding with no notice — a move National Chief Brendan Moore says has already damaged the organization’s ability to do policy work.




Moore spoke after CAP supporters marched on Parliament Hill to protest what the organization called the “Government of Canada’s unilateral decision to end the Canada-CAP Political Accord.”




The 2018 accord was signed under former prime minister Justin Trudeau after the Supreme Court of Canada’s 2016 Daniels decision, which confirmed that Métis and non-status Indians fall under federal jurisdiction. 




CAP, founded in the 1970s, is one of five national Indigenous organizations recognized by Ottawa and says it represents Métis, status and non-status First Nations people, and southern Inuit living off reserve.




“Canada has terminated its participation in the Canada-CAP Political Accord. There was no consultation with us. There was no replacement mechanism offered,” Moore said.




He said the cut landed all at once.




“It does really damage our capacity to do policy work,” he said. “For the first time in the history of CAP we never qualified for the Federal Interlocutor’s Contribution Program.”




Moore, left, marching with supporters on Parliament Hill. Photo: Keelan Jacobs/A

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: Selon des historiens autochtones, l’histoire du Québec présentée par le PQ est trompeuse
content:
Le Parti québécois (PQ) est en voie de remporter les prochaines élections provinciales du 5 octobre, et s’il y parvient, il a promis d’organiser un référendum sur l’indépendance du Québec vis-à-vis du Canada dès son premier mandat – mais il n’a pas beaucoup parlé de la place qu’occuperaient les Premières Nations et les Inuit dans ce projet.




Pendant l’année, le PQ a publié des chapitres de 

son « Livre bleu »

, un plan officiel décrivant le fonctionnement d’un Québec indépendant.




Cependant, le chapitre 22, intitulé « Relations avec les Premières Nations et les Inuit », n’est pour l’instant qu’une page blanche, accompagnée de la promesse que ce chapitre serait publié « au cours de l’été 2026 ».




APTN News a contacté le PQ pour savoir si ce chapitre était disponible, mais n’a reçu aucune réponse.




Même s’il n’y a encore rien dans le chapitre 22, le Livre bleu du PQ présente tout de même une version de l’histoire des relations entre les Français et les peuples autochtones au Québec.




Scott Berthelette, professeur métis de la Rivière-Rouge, étudie les relations entre les Français et les peuples autochtones en Nouvelle-France à l’université Queen’s. Il estime que le récit du Livre bleu du PQ simplifie à l’extrême une histoire complexe impliquant de nombreuses nations, chacune avec des intérêts différents, nouant des alliances multiples et menant des guerres.

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: PQ’s history of Quebec is misleading: Indigenous historians
content:
The Parti Québécois (PQ) is poised to win the upcoming provincial election on Oct. 5, and if they do, they have promised to call a referendum on Quebec’s independence from Canada within the first term – yet they’ve said little about how First Nations and Inuit fit into that plan. 

 




Over the past year, the PQ has been publishing chapters of 

its “Blue Book,”

 a formal plan for how an independent Quebec would function. 




However, Chapter 22, “Relations with First Nations and Inuit,” is currently a blank page with the promise that the chapter would be published “sometime in the summer of 2026.”

 




APTN News contacted the PQ to find out whether the chapter was available and received no response.







While there is nothing yet in Chapter 22, the PQ Blue Book nonetheless presents a version of the history between the French and Indigenous Peoples in Quebec.




Red River Métis history professor Scott Berthelette studies French–Indigenous relations in New France at Queen’s University. He sees the PQ Blue Book’s narrative as dramatically simplifying a complex history of many nations, each with different interests, entering multiple alliances and waging wars.

 




Berthelette told APTN that he noted in the PQ Blue Book a desire to mark the British as bad, while tying modern Francophone society in Quebec to roots predating the English conquest of Quebec.

author: Mark Blackburn
title: NAFC says friendship centres laying off staff, need $25M extra from Ottawa
content:
The head of the 

National Association of Friendship Centres

 (NAFC) says the organization needs more money to meet the needs of urban Indigenous people across the country.




At a news conference in Ottawa this week, CEO Jennifer Rankin said the lack of sustainable funding has had an effect on a number of centres.




“With this new government, there’s some education that’s needed from within, said Rankin. “Teaching people the realities of Indigenous people throughout Canada, urban Indigenous realities and letting them know and educating them on friendship centres and what we do and how we contribute to the Canadian economy and how we already are.




“The reality on that, being fiscally responsible, there were some executive directors who did have to do layoffs,” said Rankin. “We tried to cost manage and support most of our friendship centres.”




Rankin didn’t know how many people have been laid off.




Friendship Centres are the country’s largest urban Indigenous service network with more than 100 serving nearly one million people a year through employment and training, housing help, child care, health supports, cultural programming and food security.
